paragraphs: In the end, though, he began to brood over the past, and the strain was more than he could bear. Then a fine, intelligent girl caught his attention, and soon afterward he married her. He hoped that marriage would lift his lonely depression, and that if he started a new life and carefully did his duty to his wife and children, he would be free of the old memories altogether. The very opposite happened. Even in the first month of the marriage he began to be fretted constantly by the thought, “My wife loves me—but what if she knew?” When she first told him she would soon bear him a child, he was troubled. “I am giving life, but I have taken life.” Children came. “How dare I love them, teach and educate them? How can I talk to them of virtue? I have shed blood.” They were splendid children, and he longed to caress them; “and I can’t look at their innocent, candid faces. I am unworthy.”

Finally he came to be bitterly and ominously haunted by the blood of his murdered victim, by the young life he had destroyed, by the blood that cried out for vengeance. He began to have awful dreams. But he was a man of fortitude, and he bore his suffering for a long time, thinking: “I shall expiate everything by this secret agony.” That hope too was in vain. The longer it went on, the more intense his suffering became.

People respected him for his active benevolence, though everyone was overawed by his stern and gloomy character. But the more he was respected, the harder it was for him to bear. He confessed to me that he had thought of killing himself. But another idea began to haunt him—an idea he had at first thought impossible and unthinkable, though in the end it took such a hold on his heart that he could not shake it off. He dreamed of rising up, going out and confessing in front of everyone that he had committed murder. For three years this dream had pursued him, haunting him in different forms. At last he believed with his whole heart that if he confessed his crime, he would heal his soul and be at peace forever. But this belief filled his heart with terror, for how could he carry it out? And then came what happened at my duel.
“Looking at you, I have made up my mind.”
I looked at him.
“Is it possible,” I cried, clasping my hands, “that such a small thing could have led you to such a decision?”

“My resolution has been growing for the last three years,” he answered, “and your story only gave it the finishing touch. Looking at you, I reproached myself and envied you.” He said this almost sullenly.
“But you won’t be believed,” I pointed out. “It was fourteen years ago.”
“I have proof, solid proof. I will show it.”
Then I wept and kissed him.

“Tell me one thing, just one thing,” he said, as though everything depended on me. “My wife, my children! My wife may die of grief. My children won’t lose their rank or property, but they’ll be a convict’s children, and forever! And what a memory, what a memory of me I shall leave in their hearts!”
I said nothing.
“And to be parted from them, to leave them forever? It’s forever, you know, forever!”
I sat still and said a silent prayer. At last I got up. I was afraid.
“Well?” He looked at me.
“Go,” I said, “and confess. Everything passes; only the truth remains. Your children will understand, when they grow up, how noble your decision was.”

That time he left me as though his mind were made up. Yet for more than two weeks afterward he came to me every evening, still preparing himself, still unable to bring himself to the point. He made my heart ache. One day he would arrive determined and say with fervor:

“I know it will be heaven for me, heaven, the moment I confess. For fourteen years I’ve been in hell. I want to suffer. I will take my punishment and begin to live. You can go through the world doing wrong, but there’s no turning back. Now I don’t dare love my neighbor, or even my own children. Good God, perhaps my children will understand what my punishment has cost me, and they won’t condemn me! God is not in strength but in truth.”
“All will understand your sacrifice,” I said to him, “if not at once, then later; for you have served truth, the higher truth, not of the earth.”
He would go away looking comforted, but the next day he would be back, bitter, pale and sarcastic.

“Every time I come to you, you look at me so inquisitively, as if to say, ‘He still hasn’t confessed!’ Wait a bit, don’t despise me too much. It’s not as easy to do as you think. Maybe I won’t do it at all. You won’t go and inform on me then, will you?”
Far from looking at him with prying curiosity, I was afraid to look at him at all. I was sick with anxiety, and my heart was full of tears. I could not sleep at night.

“I’ve just come from my wife,” he went on. “Do you understand what the word ‘wife’ means? When I went out, the children called after me, ‘Good-by, father, hurry back to read _The Children’s Magazine_ with us.’ No, you don’t understand that! No one learns wisdom from another man’s woe.”
His eyes glittered and his lips twitched. Suddenly he struck the table with his fist so hard that everything on it jumped. He had never done such a thing before; he was such a mild man.

“But do I have to?” he exclaimed. “Must I? No one has been condemned, no one has been sent to Siberia in my place; the man died of fever. And I’ve been punished for the blood I shed by my own suffering. And I won’t be believed; they won’t believe my proofs. Do I need to confess, do I? I am ready to go on suffering all my life for the blood I have shed, if only my wife and children can be spared. Would it be just to ruin them along with me? Aren’t we making a mistake? What is right in this case? And will people see it, will they appreciate it, will they respect it?”

“Good Lord!” I thought, “he is thinking of other people’s respect at such a moment!” I felt so sorry for him then that I believe I would have shared his fate if it could have comforted him. I saw he was beside himself. I was aghast, understanding with my heart as well as my mind what such a resolution meant.
“Decide my fate!” he exclaimed again.

“Go and confess,” I whispered. My voice failed me, but I whispered it firmly. I took the New Testament from the table, the Russian translation, and showed him the Gospel of St. John, chapter 12, verse 24:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”
I had just been reading that verse when he came in. He read it.

“That’s true,” he said, but he smiled bitterly. “It’s terrible, the things you find in those books,” he said after a pause. “It’s easy enough to push them on a person. And who wrote them? Can men really have written them?”
“The Holy Spirit wrote them,” I said.
“It’s easy for you to prattle on,” he said, smiling again, this time almost with hatred.
I took the book again, opened it at another place and showed him the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10, verse 31. He read:
“It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
He read it and just flung the book down. He was trembling all over.

“An awful text,” he said. “There’s no denying you’ve chosen fitting ones.” He rose from the chair. “Well!” he said, “good-by. Perhaps I won’t come again ... we’ll meet in heaven. So I have been ‘in the hands of the living God’ for fourteen years. That is how one must think of those fourteen years. Tomorrow I will beg those hands to let me go.”
I wanted to take him in my arms and kiss him, but I did not dare. His face was twisted and dark. He went away.

“Good God,” I thought, “what has he gone off to face!” I fell on my knees before the ikon and wept for him before the Holy Mother of God, our swift defender and helper. I spent half an hour praying in tears. It was late, about midnight. Suddenly I saw the door open and he came in again. I was surprised.
“Where have you been?” I asked him.
“I think,” he said, “I’ve forgotten something ... my handkerchief, I think.... Well, even if I haven’t forgotten anything, let me stay a little.”
He sat down. I stood over him.
“You sit down too,” he said.
I sat down. We sat in silence for two minutes. He looked intently at me and suddenly smiled (I remembered that), then got up, embraced me warmly and kissed me.
“Remember how I came to you a second time,” he said. “Do you hear? Remember it!”
And he went out.
“Tomorrow,” I thought.

And so it was. That evening I did not know that the next day was his birthday. I had not been out for the last few days, so I had no chance of hearing it from anyone. On that day he always held a great gathering, and everyone in the town went to it. It was the same this time. After dinner he walked into the middle of the room with a paper in his hand—a formal declaration to the chief of his department, who was present. He read this declaration aloud to the whole assembly. It contained a full account of the crime, in every detail.
“I cut myself off from men as a monster. God has visited me,” he said in conclusion. “I want to suffer for my sin!”

Then he brought out and laid on the table all the things he had kept for fourteen years, thinking they would prove his crime: the jewels of the murdered woman, which he had stolen to divert suspicion; a cross and a locket taken from her neck, with a portrait of her betrothed inside the locket; her notebook; and two letters. One was from her betrothed, telling her that he would soon be with her, and the other was her unfinished answer, left on the table to be sent off next day. He had carried off these two letters—what for? Why had he kept them for fourteen years afterward, instead of destroying them as evidence against him?

And this is what happened. Everyone was amazed and horrified. Everyone refused to believe it and thought he was deranged, though all listened with intense curiosity. A few days later it was fully decided and agreed in every house that the unhappy man was mad. The legal authorities could not refuse to take up the case, but they too dropped it. The trinkets and letters made them think, but they decided that even if these turned out to be genuine, no charge could be based on them alone. Besides, she might have given him those things as a friend, or asked him to keep them safe for her. I heard afterward, however, that the friends and relations of the murdered woman proved the things were genuine, and that there was no doubt about them. Yet nothing, after all, was destined to come of it.

Five days later, everyone had heard that he was ill and that his life was in danger. I cannot explain the nature of his illness; they said it was a heart ailment. But it became known that his wife had persuaded the doctors to examine his mental condition too, and that they had concluded it was a case of insanity. I betrayed nothing, though people ran to question me. But when I wanted to visit him, I was forbidden to for a long while, above all by his wife.

“You are the one who caused his illness,” she said to me. “He was always gloomy, but for the last year people noticed that he was oddly excited and did strange things. And now you have ruined him. Your preaching has brought him to this. For the last month he was always with you.”

Indeed, not only his wife but the whole town was down on me and blamed me. “It’s all your doing,” they said. I was silent, and in fact I rejoiced at heart, for I saw plainly God’s mercy to the man who had turned against himself and punished himself. I could not believe he was insane.

At last they let me see him; he insisted on saying good-by to me. I went in to him and saw at once that not only his days but his hours were numbered. He was weak and yellow, his hands trembled, he gasped for breath, but his face was full of tender, happy feeling.
“It is done!” he said. “I’ve been longing to see you for so long. Why didn’t you come?”
I did not tell him that they had refused to let me see him.

“God has had pity on me and is calling me to Himself. I know I am dying, but I feel joy and peace for the first time after so many years. There was heaven in my heart from the moment I did what I had to do. Now I dare to love my children and to kiss them. Neither my wife nor the judges nor anyone has believed it. My children will never believe it either. I see in that God’s mercy to them. I shall die, and my name will be without a stain for them. And now I feel God near, my heart rejoices as in Heaven ... I have done my duty.”
He could not speak. He gasped for breath and pressed my hand warmly, looking at me fervently. We did not talk for long, because his wife kept peeping in at us. But he had time to whisper to me:
“Do you remember how I came back to you that second time, at midnight? I told you to remember it. Do you know what I came back for? I came to kill you!”
I gave a start.

“I went out from you then into the darkness and wandered about the streets, struggling with myself. And suddenly I hated you so much that I could hardly bear it. Now, I thought, he is all that binds me, and he is my judge. I can’t refuse to face my punishment tomorrow, for he knows everything. It wasn’t that I was afraid you would betray me (I never even thought of that). I thought, ‘How can I look him in the face if I don’t confess?’ And if you had been at the other end of the earth, but alive, it would have been all the same. The thought was unendurable that you were alive, knowing everything and condemning me. I hated you as though you were the cause, as though you were to blame for everything. I came back to you then, remembering that you had a dagger lying on your table. I sat down and asked you to sit down, and for a whole minute I thought it over. If I had killed you, that murder would have ruined me even if I had not confessed the other. But I didn’t think about that at all, and I didn’t want to think of it at that moment. I only hated you and longed to take revenge on you for everything. The Lord conquered the devil in my heart. But let me tell you, you were never nearer death.”

A week later he died. The whole town followed him to the grave. The chief priest made a speech full of feeling. Everyone lamented the terrible illness that had cut short his days. But after the funeral the whole town was up in arms against me, and people even refused to see me. Some, at first a few and later more, did begin to believe his story. They visited me and questioned me with great interest and eagerness, for man loves to see the downfall and disgrace of the righteous. But I held my tongue, and very soon afterward I left the town. Five months later, by God’s grace, I entered upon the safe and blessed path, praising the unseen finger that had guided me to it so clearly. But to this day I remember in my prayers the servant of God, Mihail, who suffered so greatly.
